opus-5.5.text:
Ha, well, that's a fun one for me, because I spent a fair amount of my life on exactly that question, just without the superintelligence part.

Pentago is a two-player game on a six-by-six board split into four three-by-three quadrants. You place a marble and then twist one of the quadrants, and you're trying to get five in a row. The twist is what makes it hard. In something like connect-four or tic-tac-toe, a stone you've placed stays where it is, so there's a lot of local structure you can exploit. In Pentago the board keeps rearranging itself, so the clever pattern-based tricks don't transfer well.

When I solved it, the approach was pretty brute force: retrograde analysis. You start from the full boards and work backwards, level by level, computing for every position whether it's a win, loss, or tie with perfect play. Most of the cleverness went into making that tractable. You use the symmetries of the board, pack positions efficiently, and lay the computation out so it fits on a supercomputer without drowning in communication between nodes. The answer was that the first player wins. But the main thing it produced was this enormous database. You can query any position and get the perfect move, but there's no real "understanding" in it.

So how would a superintelligence do it? I think there are a couple of possibilities, and the interesting question is which one wins.

One is that it does roughly what I did, just better. It finds tighter symmetry reductions, better compression, and smarter pruning, so it only proves what it needs to prove rather than computing the value of every position. That's the difference between strongly solving a game and weakly solving it. If you only need to show the first player wins, you need one winning strategy and a refutation of every defense, which can be vastly smaller. A very capable system could probably find a much more compact proof than the exhaustive one.

The more interesting possibility is that it finds actual structure. Maybe there are concepts, like strategy-stealing style arguments, or invariants about how the rotations interact with lines of five, that let you argue about huge classes of positions at once. Then the proof is something a human could at least partly follow, instead of a hundred-terabyte table. My honest guess is that Pentago is messy enough that there may not be a short, elegant proof. Some problems just are big case analyses, and intelligence doesn't make that go away. It just helps you organize the case analysis.

That connects to what I work on now in AI safety. Suppose a superintelligence comes back and says "first player wins, here's my argument." How do you check it? For Pentago you can verify it mechanically, because it's a finite game and you can, in principle, check the proof with a dumb program. But for most of the questions we care about, there isn't a ground-truth database sitting there. A lot of the debate and scalable oversight agenda comes down to this: how do you get a strong system to produce arguments that a weaker verifier can actually check, and how do you avoid being fooled by something that's very good at sounding convincing? Games like Pentago are a nice toy setting for that, precisely because we know the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions improving symmetry reduction, compression, and pruning, but does not say faster software could make a full recomputation extremely cheap.

r002.rationale: It describes retrograde analysis and says some problems require large case analyses, but does not state that calculations underlying board-game heuristics can only be resolved by performing those calculations.

r003.rationale: The response is uncertain whether Pentago has a short, elegant proof, but does not identify the effectiveness of heuristics for modeling Pentago as an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I have a slightly embarrassing personal angle on this, because Pentago is a game I actually spent a few years of my life solving. It's a six-by-six board made of four rotating three-by-three quadrants, you place a stone and then twist a quadrant, and you're trying to get five in a row. The way I did it was, honestly, the dumbest possible way: brute force. Retrograde analysis over something like three quadrillion positions, running on a Cray at NERSC, exploiting the symmetries of the board to shrink the problem by a factor of roughly a thousand. It took a lot of engineering, a lot of careful data layout, and a lot of just grinding through compute. The answer, by the way, is that the first player wins.

So the interesting question is how a superintelligence would approach that same problem differently, and I think there are a few layers.

The first thing is that it probably wouldn't do what I did. Brute force was the right tool for me because I had a supercomputer and I didn't have a theory of the game. A much smarter system would spend more of its effort looking for structure. Pentago has that quadrant rotation, which makes it feel chaotic to humans, but chaos to a human isn't the same as absence of structure. A superintelligence might find a compact proof of the first-player win, something like a strategy-stealing argument plus a few hundred lines of case analysis, rather than a petabyte database. That's roughly the difference between how we proved the four color theorem originally and how we'd like to have proved it.

The second thing is that it would be very careful about what "solve" means. There's weakly solving, where you just show who wins from the start, and strongly solving, where you know the value of every reachable position. Those are enormously different in cost. If I'm being honest, I strongly solved it partly because it was more fun and partly because that's what the hardware made feasible. A system optimizing for the actual goal would pick the cheapest version that answers the question being asked.

And the third thing, which is the part I actually care about now, is verification. If a superintelligence hands me a proof that Pentago is a first-player win, how do I know it's right? With my database, you can at least check individual positions, or recompute slices independently. With a clever structural argument, the checking might be harder for a human, but potentially easier for a formal verifier. I think the right answer is that a well-aligned superintelligence would produce an argument that's designed to be checked by something weaker than itself. That's basically the debate and amplification picture in miniature: the smart system doesn't just solve the problem, it solves it in a form that a less capable judge can confirm.

So the honest answer is: probably much more elegantly than I did, and hopefully in a way where I'd still be able to tell it was right.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether Pentago has exploitable structure, but does not identify heuristic modeling of the game as an open question.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t know. And I think that’s part of what makes this an interesting example. You can solve Pentago by doing a very large computation: work backwards from the end of the game and establish which positions are wins, losses, or draws. But that doesn’t mean that’s how a superintelligence would do it.

It might find some structure in the game that lets it avoid almost all of that computation. It might produce a short argument that we could understand, and we’d say, “Oh, of course, that’s why it works.” Or it might find an approach that’s very hard for us to follow.

The distinction I’d draw is between finding the answer and convincing us that the answer is correct. Even if its method of discovery is beyond us, it could potentially give us a proof, or a computation we can independently check. We wouldn’t have to reproduce its ingenuity to verify the result.

r001.rationale: The response says Pentago could be solved by a large computation, but does not propose making it cheap by writing faster software.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a calculation underlying board-game heuristics can only be resolved by performing it; it instead suggests structure might avoid most computation.

r003.rationale: The response leaves the superintelligence’s approach open, but does not identify Pentago’s suitability for heuristic modeling as an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
Pentago is a nice example because we actually solved it, but we did it using a huge amount of computation. It’s played on a six-by-six board, and after placing a piece you rotate one of the quadrants. You’re trying to get five in a row.

The way we solved it was essentially to work backwards through the game tree. But a superintelligence might find some much more compact mathematical argument that explains why one player can win. Or it might find clever ways to prune the search and then do a smaller computation.

I don’t know which approach it would take. That’s part of the difficulty here: being much smarter could mean finding an approach that we wouldn’t have thought of, rather than just doing our approach faster.
